verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents. To YHWH, in the distress to me, I called, and he answered me.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing. Out of the tight place I cried — to the LORD, to no one else — and he answered me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open on the cry already finished: the psalmist speaks from the far side of rescue, and that is what makes everything after it a plea rather than a panic. The Hebrew order puts the destination first, 'to YHWH', before the distress, before the 'I'; actors should land on the name. The pointing of 'in the distress' (batzaratah) carries an old-fashioned ending that Radak and Meiri read as intensifying, 'in the great distress'. 'Distress' here is literally narrowness, a tight place, the opposite of the wide space of rescue.

The title is part of the verse in the Hebrew, which is why the KJV numbers it 120:0. 'Song of degrees' is the KJV's Latinate rendering of 'steps'; the Hebrew word is maʿalot, 'ascents'. The tradition gives three answers, and a director should choose one: the fifteen temple steps on which the Levites sang one psalm per step (Rashi and Radak, citing Sukkah), the pilgrims' climb up to Jerusalem, or the rising out of exile (Radak's second reading). Fifteen psalms, 120 to 134, carry the title. KJV 'he heard me' softens the verb: the Hebrew is 'he answered', which is a response, not just a hearing.

philological_notes.note: 'The ascents', from the verb 'to go up'. It can mean steps, pilgrim journeys or the going up from exile; the superscription is shared by Psalms 120–134.
'In the distress', literally in the narrowness. The extra he ending is read by Radak as marking the greatness of the distress.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, deliver my self from a lip of falsehood, from a tongue of deceit.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD — pull my life out of reach of the lying lip, the tongue that smiles and deceives.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the speaker is in the present, and the prayer is a single breathless imperative: 'deliver'. The 'nefesh' is not a soul in the later, ethereal sense; it is the throat, the life, the self that can be strangled or slandered. KJV 'soul' is right for the old English word but misleads a modern ear. 'Lip' and 'tongue' are the Hebrew's body parts for speech, and they stand for people: Rashi hears 'the seed of the wicked' who trap others by their mouths, Meiri the enemies who plot.

In a courtroom culture of oaths and witnesses, a lying lip could kill; false testimony was as lethal as a weapon, which is what the next verses build on. The KJV's 'lying lips' makes the noun plural and adjectival; the Hebrew has the singular 'lip of falsehood' and 'tongue of deceit' as two nouns in construct chains. Note that 'deceit' (remiyah) is the word for slack or treacherous, the same root as a drooping bow that shoots wide.

philological_notes.note: 'Deceit', also the word for a slack, unreliable bow in other texts; here the tongue is a weapon that misses its stated target. The bow connection is a lexicon observation I am not citing page by page.
'My self', literally my throat or life; it is the whole person as a living, breathing, vulnerable being.

verses.translation_literal: What will [He] give to you, and what will [He] add to you, tongue of deceit?
verses.translation_dramatic: And what will He give you for it, O tongue? What more will He lay upon you, smooth tongue, tongue of deceit?
verses.directors_commentary:
Turn to the tongue and speak to it directly: the psalmist stops talking about the liar and addresses the organ itself, as if it were a person standing in the dock. The question is a threat in the form of an open hand. 'What will He give you, and what more will He add?' The Hebrew leaves the giver unnamed, and the line may echo the oath-curse pattern ('so may God do to you, and more also'), where 'give' and 'add' name a punishment and its doubling. That is a reading, not something the text states; the sentence works just as well as a taunt asking what profit the lie can possibly bring.

The KJV hedges twice. It turns the active verbs into passives ('shall be given', 'shall be done') and so loses the sense that someone is acting, and it renders the second verb, which is simply 'add', as 'what shall be done', which softens the escalation. It also gives 'false tongue' for lashon remiyyah, 'tongue of deceit', where remiyyah is the slack, treacherous quality of a bow that will not shoot straight. Play the last two words as a verdict. The tradition reads the line in two ways: Rashi takes the giver to be God and 'add' to mean guards and partitions, so that the tongue is already fenced behind two walls; Metzudat David asks what further guard could be placed on a tongue already set behind the wall of lips and teeth.

philological_notes.translit: mah yitten lekha umah yosif lakh
philological_notes.note: 'What will he give you, and what will he add to you?' The paired verbs 'give' and 'add' may echo the oath-curse pattern ('so may God do to you and more also'), but this is a possible echo only. Rashi reads the unnamed giver as God and 'add' as guards and partitions (the tongue lies behind two walls); Metzudat David reads it as asking what further guard could be set on a tongue already enclosed by lips and teeth; Malbim reads it as 'what benefit or gain will this bring you'.

Deceit, treachery. The same word is used for a slack bow that shoots wide of its mark, which gives the picture of a tongue that looks ready but betrays the one who trusts it. The bow sense is from the lexica, not from this verse.

verses.translation_literal: Arrows of a warrior, sharpened, with coals of broom plants.
verses.translation_dramatic: Arrows from a soldier's hand, whetted to a point — and under them, the red glow of broom-wood coals.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to the question of verse 3 is a pair of images, delivered fast and without a verb. The first is the warrior's arrow, sharpened, flying from a distance. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as the tongue that kills from far away; Malbim, as the whisper behind a man's back. The second is the broom coal: the root of 'rotem', a desert shrub whose charcoal burns hot and long. Meiri and Rashi's tradition (Genesis Rabbah) say it stays alight inside after the outside looks dead, so a man who picks up the ash is burned. That is the friendly liar: the flattery looks safe and is still burning.

KJV and ASV 'juniper' follows an old guess; modern botany points to the white broom, a desert bush. Note 'mighty one' for gibbor, a champion, rather than the KJV's flat 'the mighty'. Directors should hear the dual image as ranged and close: the arrow strikes at a distance, the coal in the hand.

philological_notes.note: Broom plants (Retama raetam). KJV and ASV translate 'juniper'. Its charcoal proverbially burns long and stays hot inside after looking cold.
'Sharpened', the same verb used of sharpening a sword or whetting the tongue (Ps 64:4).

verses.translation_literal: Woe to me, that I have sojourned [in] Meshech, I have dwelt with the tents of Kedar.
verses.translation_dramatic: Woe to me! I have lived as a stranger in Meshech; I have pitched my life beside the black tents of Kedar.
verses.directors_commentary:
A cry of exile, and a geographical joke that is not meant to be funny. Meshech is a people of the far north, in Anatolia, near the Black Sea; Kedar is the Arabian desert tribe of the south-east, nomads of black goat-hair tents. No one lives in both. The pairing marks the two extremes of the known world: the speaker is a stranger everywhere, among everyone who is foreign. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take this as the Jewish exile among the nations; Rashi as the many exiles of Israel. The KJV's 'I sojourn in Mesech' is fair, but 'dwell in the tents of Kedar' softens the preposition 'with': the Hebrew says 'with the tents', which treats the tents as people.

The verb 'sojourn' (gur) is the status of a resident alien with no land and no legal protection: in the ancient Near East, an outsider depended on the host's goodwill for water, food and safety. 'Woe' (oyah) is a rare, plaintive form of 'oy'. Play the line with the sound of the name 'Meshech', which also means 'drawing out', as Radak and Meiri hear it: a long, dragged-out stay.

philological_notes.note: 'I have sojourned', to live as a resident alien (ger) without land rights or tribal protection.
Meshech, a northern people listed among the sons of Japheth (Gen 10:2). The same consonants mean 'drawing out', a long time; Meiri and Radak hear the pun on the long exile.
Kedar, a son of Ishmael and a tribe of Arabian nomads whose tents were of dark goat hair; the name echoes 'dark'.

verses.translation_literal: Much has my self dwelt for itself with one who hates peace.
verses.translation_dramatic: Too long, far too long, my life has made its home with those who hate peace.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb of the last verse returns, 'dwelt', and with it the sense of an unwanted neighbour. The line opens with the word 'much' (rabbat), and the actor should lean on it: it is both 'a great deal' and 'too long'. Ibn Ezra and Radak note the final tav as standing for a he, a feminine adverbial form meaning 'for a long time', and Meiri says the same. The 'one who hates peace' is singular in Hebrew where the KJV and BBE vary between 'him' and 'the haters'; it is a participle used as a category, 'the peace-hater', and a director may choose whether it is a person or a people.

The small word 'for herself' (lah) is a reflexive dative: the self has settled itself in, which makes the tragedy sharper, since the speaker has half accepted the home. Malbim reads this as worse than Meshech and Kedar because the haters of peace are the speaker's own kin. Others hear the tents of verse 5 as the hostile neighbour: those peoples hate peace in the same way.

philological_notes.note: 'Much, long': a feminine adjective with an adverbial sense, with the final tav read as a he, as in the feminine form of the word for much.
'One who hates peace', a participle used for a person or class defined by that trait.

verses.translation_literal: I [am] peace, and when I speak, they [are] for the war.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am peace. I only have to open my mouth, and they are already marching to war.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes on its sharpest line and its simplest grammar: 'I peace' (no verb), 'they for the war' (no verb). Two clauses, each a bare noun, set against each other. KJV 'I am for peace' is a gloss: the Hebrew says 'I am peace', and Ibn Ezra explains that this is the idiom 'I am a man of peace', like 'and I am prayer' (Ps 109:4). Rashi and Radak: when I speak peace to them, they come to fight me.

The irony closes the circle of the psalm. The speaker began by being delivered from a lying tongue; now the speaker's own tongue, speaking honestly, is the thing that provokes. The line ends on 'war' (milchamah), the word it has set against 'peace' (shalom), and the psalm stops there without resolution. Malbim adds the sting: the speaker's inside matches the outside, while theirs do not. Play it quietly. No shouting; the speaker is exhausted.

philological_notes.note: 'I am peace', a verbless clause meaning 'I am a person of peace', as Ibn Ezra compares 'I [am] prayer'.
'For the war', with the definite article; war is the thing they stand ready for, as against peace.
